object.content:
TIL: CDNs minimize latency for clients far from the original server because no matter how far away the client is, there's always a CDN node close to them

CDN stands for content delivery network; CDNs are networks of geographically distributed servers that fetch and cache assets from the original server more efficiently; they save client bandwidth and reduce the original server load; always consider CDNs on global scale

#softwareengineer

object.content:
TIL: every CDN server has its own local cache with two main strategies to populate it

pull CDN (most common): lazily fetches content, requires low maintenance, but the first request is slower and assets can become stale. cache busting helps if we don't want stale content

push CDN: requires engineering effort to propagate updates to the CDN caches; the first request is fast bc CDN server doesn't need to travel to the original server. more control over cache timing

#softwareengineer #cdn

TIL: about memory management

systems allocate and free up memory during the execution of a program; older languages like c and c++, don't have automatically memory management, so programmers needs to explicit do the management; one allocation = one deallocation; uses RAM, but also CPU registers, CPU cache and disk space (virtual memory)

#devlife #memorymanagement

object.content:
TIL: about memory leak

it's when an allocated memory is not deallocated and the OS can't reclaim it; the memory became unusable until the program/system terminates; on long-running programs, over time memory leaks causes the program run out of memory and crash; if accidentally deallocate memory previously deallocated it might end up deallocating memory that is in use, causing security vulnerabilities and unpredictable and disastrous consequences

#devlife #memorymanagement

object.content:
TIL: system detects programs running low on memory, it pauses program execution & runs garbage collector

GC gets all in-use memory, compacts heap by moving it to beginning, updates references to new locations & releases unreachable memory; optimizes by identifying short-lived vs persistent memory using "generations"; long-lived memory surviving multiple GC runs gets cleared less frequently; it causes random pauses during program execution; less suitable for real-time apps

#memorymanagement

object.content:
TIL: automatic memory management with reference counting

each allocated memory has a reference count; when program variables refer to it, count goes up; when they stop, count decreases; if count == 0, memory gets freed; requires extra space per object to store the count; good for real-time apps; requires programmer to be conscious about creating reference cycles, which cause memory leaks

#memorymanagement #devlife

TIL: ruby, a dynamically typed language, does benefit from static type checking

ruby type checking occurs in runtime; ruby 3 has .rbs files that contains the type information; it provides several degrees of type checking; you can use type profiler to detect type conflicts

ruby wants the benefits of static type checking and does so at some levels. it doesn't want declarations which, for ruby, are redundant, and instead abstracts them away

object.content:
TIL: should I use single or double quotes in git commit messages?

both works fine, but go for the single quotes; double quotes might trigger "command substitution" on unix-like systems

for example:

```bash
$ echo "`ls`"

./docs/
./node_modules/
./package-lock.json
./package.json
./pages/
./README.md
```

#git #devlife #learninginpublic

object.content:
TIL: why n+1 is bad?

network latency = 1 query travels over the internet. when db in different geographic loc, it matter significantly; framework overhead = rails internals does lot of work backward/forward per query; db cost = parse, plan, execute and return per query; framework overhead + db cost = CPU and I/O server spikes; connection pool = db connection is expensive and hold connection is bad for concurrent envs

we really want to talk little to db!
